newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Afghan chaos setback for landlocked Central Asia.
newsitem.headline: Afghan chaos setback for landlocked Central Asia.

text.p: The Taleban militia may be in retreat but Central Asian leaders, opposed to their purist brand of Islam, said on Monday that fighting in Afghanistan still threatened stability and their economic interests in the region.

"The danger of the war spreading exists," Islam Karimov, president of the former Soviet republic of Uzbekistan, told journalists in Almaty during an official two-day visit to the neighbouring Kazakh capital.

Former Soviet states in Central Asia reinforced security on their borders with Afghanistan last month when Taleban took Mazar-i-Sharif, northern stronghold of ethnic Uzbek warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

When the Taleban were driven out shortly afterwards, ex-communist leaders in Central Asia breathed a sigh of relief as the militia's strict brand of Islam was pushed back, along with the threat of a potentially destabilising refuge crisis.

"In Afghanistan, the Taleban is only one of several warring factions," Karimov said, the region's most vocal critic of the black-turbanned militia. "They must give up trying to decide matters through military means."

Najibullah Zia Rahman, head of the Afghan embassy in Almaty which is loyal to ousted Afghan president Burhanuddin Rabbani, told journalists the anti-Taleban alliance's fortunes would improve. "Very soon the balance will turn in favour of the alliance," he said.

Made up mostly of the Uzbek Dostum's forces and those of ethnic Tajik commander Ahmad Shah Masood, both groups can look to kin across the borders in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. The alliance, seen as a bulwark against fundamentalism, is quietly backed by Moscow and most of ex-Soviet Central Asia.

Yet while relieved that the Taleban have suffered a reverse, the chaos that has ensued has brought landlocked Central Asia, which sees a unified and stable Afghanistan as a potential route for oil and gas exports, back to square one.
Central Asian states are anxious to break their dependence on their former colonial master Moscow for their limited access to Soviet-era oil and gas pipelines.

An ambitious plan by U.S. Unocal Corp and Saudi Arabia's Delta Oil to build a $2 billion gas pipeline from ex-Soviet Turkmenistan to Pakistan via Afghanistan will remain on the drawing board as long as fighting continues to rock the mountainous republic.
Diplomats have said that for Unocal, order under the victorious Taleban was its best hope of a stable Afghanistan.

"We have an interest in peace for Afghanistan," Kasymzhomart Tokayev, energy-rich Kazakhstan's foreign minister, told reporters during Karimov's visit. "We naturally have an interest in the transport of oil and gas through Afghanistan.
Uzbekistan's Karimov called on unnamed "outside forces" to stop what he said their interference in the Afghan war.
Central Asian leaders were irritated by Pakistan's rapid recognition of Taleban rule and suspect it of aiding the militia. Pakistan says it is neutral in the fighting.

Whatever the vital interests at stake, however, Karimov warned that the Central Asian states must not get sucked in to a new "Afghan adventure", a reference to the Soviet Union's disastrous intervention in Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989.
